papers.title: PIVOT: Distribution-Preserving Multi-BitWatermarking with Minimax-Optimal Scoring
papers.abstract: As LLM-generated content becomes increasingly widespread, reliable attribution calls for multi-bit watermarks that embed recoverable messages without distorting the output distribution. We introduce PIVOT, a multi-bit watermark with model-free verification based on mirrored rank-interval sampling. At each generation step, PIVOT uses a keyed pseudorandom scalar and a secret permutation of the vocabulary. The message bit determines whether next-token probability intervals are arranged in forward or reverse secret-rank order. Sampling from these mirrored layouts preserves every token probability exactly while inducing an opposite-signed dependence between the scalar and the sampled token's secret rank. This dependence yields a pivotal rank statistic whose null distribution is invariant to the unknown next-token law, enabling model-free calibration and decoding. We formulate joint watermark detection and message recovery as a multiple-hypothesis testing problem, derive a moment-robust minimax-optimal detection score over a relaxed moment class, and establish finite-sample recovery guarantees. Extensive experiments on two representative large language models validate the effectiveness of PIVOT, demonstrating reliable watermark detection and message recovery while preserving the generator's output distribution.

papers.title: LIC-Audit: How Comparable Are Reported Gains in Learned Image Compression?
papers.abstract: Learned image compression (LIC) papers often report BD-rate improvements of only a few percent. They are measured against VTM reference software whose version keeps changing: the claims we audit name 7 versions, 5 in 2025 papers alone. But how comparable are these numbers across papers, and what evidence should future papers give for such small gains? We introduce LIC-Audit, an analysis of 353 released rate-distortion curves from 36 repositories, and a controlled re-evaluation of eight public codec releases with 28,193 encode-decode records. We identify three problems. First, different VTM reference runs change BD-rates by up to 3.56 percentage points, and on CLIC Pro published numbers order 10 of 55 method pairs differently from a common computation; comparing codecs directly over a fixed quality range removes this dependence. Second, releases use different and mostly undocumented conventions for counting bits, computing PSNR, and padding images. Under consistent measurement, the GLIC method's 1.00% lead over the HPCM method on Tecnick becomes a 1.43% deficit, changing only the padding reverses the comparison of HPCM and CMIC, and most gaps narrow when MS-SSIM replaces PSNR. Third, average curves hide how much results vary from image to image, so whether a small gain is statistically significant depends on the assumed variation. An optimistic assumption calls 12.0% of comparisons between equally good codecs significant on test sets as small as Kodak, instead of 5%; a cautious one leaves 18 of 45 differences between recent codecs undecided, yet per-image results show 12 of them to be significant. Beyond auditing past results, LIC-Audit provides a versioned evaluation protocol, a public leaderboard website with a scoring tool, source-linked benchmark data, per-image measurements, and reporting guidelines, to help future LIC papers make comparable and verifiable claims of progress.

papers.title: CAFE-AQI: Coverage-Aware Day-Ahead AQI Forecasting with Early Warning and Conformal Uncertainty in Bangladesh
papers.abstract: Next-day air quality forecasting often assumes city records are equally complete and independent. However, an audit of a large Bangladesh dataset revealed a sharp coverage expansion after August 2022 and showed that 103 city labels correspond to only 61 unique AQI trajectories. To address these issues, this paper presents CAFE-AQI, a coverage-aware framework for forecasting next-day maximum AQI. It also estimates the probability of Unhealthy-or-worse conditions (AQI >= 151). Data were divided chronologically into training (2022-2023), calibration (2024), and testing (2025). To prevent duplicate records from dominating training and evaluation, identical trajectories were weighted. The framework combines temporal and pollutant features with a five-neighbor spatial context. It also includes a class-balanced warning head and risk-conditional conformal calibration aimed at providing early warnings and prediction intervals. Evaluation on the duplicate-balanced 2025 data gave an MAE of 9.76, an RMSE of 15.04, and an R-squared value of 0.910 for CAFE-AQI. Its MAE was 3.63 AQI lower than persistence (95% CI: 3.49-3.76), with lower errors in each of the 61 trajectory groups. For unhealthy-air warnings, the F1-score was 0.908 and the AUROC was 0.982. The nominal 90% intervals covered 92.09% of observations. When an entire spatial block was excluded from training, the MAE remained 10.66, showing that the lightweight model transferred reasonably well to unseen locations.

papers.title: From Data to Action: Accelerating Refinery Optimization with AI
papers.abstract: Nowadays refinery optimization utilizes sheer amounts of data, which can be handled with modern Linear Programming (LP) software, but the interpreting and applying the results remains challenging. Large petrochemical companies use massive models, with hundreds of thousands of input matrix elements. The LP solution is mathematically correct, but simplifications are made in the model, and data supply errors may occur. Therefore, further insight is needed to trust the results. The novelty of the paper consists of enhancing the LP solver with a memory, which makes possible to find potential errors in the input data, finding unusual relations in the data on different decision levels, by introducing an anomaly detection tool. Analyzing the potential "anomalies" in the input and output of LP, the subsequent LP solutions can be improved. The Anomaly Detection tool proposed comprises three methodologies. A transformed version of the popular ECOD methodology is applied. New methods are proposed to handle high-dimensional data: choosing the most informative pairs. Then, this is used alongside two 2D Anomaly Detection algorithms, revealing several business opportunities and data supply errors in the MOL refinery scheduling and planning architecture. The proposed tool learns connections in past data and runs very efficiently on present data revealing unusual connections sorted by their importance. Up to this step, optimization and Anomaly Detection happened automatically, and thereafter, decision makers may take a look at the most relevant anomalies found, and decide how to further improve the subsequent LPs. The tool also has periodic retraining built in.

papers.title: Developing a Subdistrict-Level Economic Progress Index Using Geospatial Data
papers.abstract: This paper develops an Economic Progress Index (EPI), a composite measure built from Earth Observation (EO) and open geospatial data with unsupervised Principal Component Analysis (PCA) weighting. The index captures the observable productive and enabling capacity of local economies and the intensity with which economic space is used. Sub-national monitoring in developing economies is held back by sparse data: district GDP estimates arrive with multi-year lags, rely on price deflators and top-down allocation, and do not exist at the subdistrict (taluka/tehsil) scale where place-based policy is targeted. The EPI fuses multi-sensor satellite data, gridded population and OpenStreetMap road and amenity networks across 357 subdistricts of Maharashtra, India, over 46 quarters (2015 Q1 - 2026 Q2). Seasonal-Trend decomposition using LOESS (STL) separates long-run trends from monsoon and crop-cycle seasonality. A non-negative PCA gives sign-consistent, interpretable weights and rankings nearly identical to standard PCA ($\rho$ = 0.998). Across districts, the index explains 74% of the variation in the NFHS-5 wealth index, 52% in household consumption (HCES 2023-24) and about 78% in real district GDP levels (65% in logs), but does not track short-run output growth. Because it measures structural capacity rather than annual output, the index kept rising through the FY2020-21 COVID-19 contraction. Across Maharashtra's six revenue divisions, relative inequality fell by 44% even as the absolute gap between leading and lagging divisions widened by 32%; district-level $\beta$-convergence implies a half-life of about 14 years. The framework offers a scalable, deflator-free basis for structural monitoring in data-sparse economies.

papers.title: The Structural Number of Parties: An Electoral-Outcome-Independent Baseline for Comparing Party-System Scale
papers.abstract: How many parties can a country structurally sustain? Standard measures such as the effective number of parties (ENP) cannot answer this question. They are descriptive and post hoc: they summarize competition only after an election, and they depend on electoral returns that are often missing, interrupted, or unreliable in many developing democracies, particularly in Africa. They also offer no common scale for comparing the size of party registers with realized electoral fragmentation. We introduce the Structural Number of Parties (SNP), an outcome-independent baseline derived from two universally available quantities: population size and territorial area. Building on the logic of the seat product model and the cube-root law of assembly size, the SNP gives an ex ante benchmark that can be computed for any country and year, including where electoral data are absent. Applied to African states, the SNP enables a structural gap diagnosis that distinguishes under-fragmented systems, marked by hegemonic-party dominance, from over-fragmented ones, marked by excessive atomization. The framework thus provides a transparent and reproducible tool to inform institutional reform and the rationalization of party systems across the continent.

papers.title: Statistical Performance Guarantee for Subgroup Identification with Generic Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Across a wide array of disciplines, many researchers use machine learning (ML) algorithms to identify a subgroup of individuals who are likely to benefit from a treatment the most (``exceptional responders'') or those who are harmed by it. A common approach to this subgroup identification problem consists of two steps. First, researchers estimate the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) using an ML algorithm. Next, they use the estimated CATE to select those individuals who are predicted to be most affected by the treatment, either positively or negatively. Unfortunately, CATE estimates are often biased and noisy. In addition, utilizing the same data to both identify a subgroup and estimate its group average treatment effect results in a multiple testing problem. To address these challenges, we develop uniform confidence bands for estimation of the group average treatment effect sorted by generic ML algorithm (GATES). Using these uniform confidence bands, researchers can identify, with a statistical guarantee, a subgroup whose GATES exceeds a certain effect size, regardless of how this effect size is chosen. The proposed methodology uses random treatment assignment, random sampling of units, and continuity and moment conditions, without requiring consistency or monotonicity of the ML score. We derive a Wiener representation of the estimation error, with corrections for the empirical subgroup threshold and the fixed treatment sample size. Estimating this representation gives asymptotically exact uniform coverage using Gaussian draws, without refitting the ML model. We also develop uniform bands for mean-adjusted treatment effects and other evaluation metrics. A simulation design and an application to a clinical trial of late-stage prostate cancer illustrate the subgroup identification problem.

papers.title: Global sensitivity analysis of transient regimes in non-Newtonian dam-break flows applied in rheometry
papers.abstract: Non-Newtonian dam-break flows are a classical problem with numerous engineering applications. These flows are particularly important in alternative rheometry, where they are used to rapidly and affordably estimate rheological properties, such as in the slump test and Bostwick consistometer test. However, the lifting dynamics of the containing obstacle introduce inertial effects that can compromise the accurate estimation of these properties. These effects are influenced by the lifting velocity, the fluid's viscosity, and the initial geometry of the sample. This study aims to quantify the influence of lifting velocity and to provide physical insights into how inertial effects influence the flow. A global sensitivity analysis (GSA) framework adapted for functional outputs (e.g., time series) is employed, using data generated from high-fidelity simulations with ANSYS Fluent. The GSA produces sensitivity curves that track the evolving importance of each input parameter over time. Three distinct flow regimes are identified, namely mobilization, transition and viscous regimes, each governed by different dominant factors. The first two regimes are significantly affected by the lifting velocity, revealing the influence of inertial effects, whereas the viscous regime is dominated by fluid rheology and shows a increasing importance of the yield stress. These results are contextualized in terms of traditional rheometry tests.

papers.title: A probabilistic analysis of the Brumadinho tailings dam-breach using uncertainty quantification and global sensitivity analysis
papers.abstract: On 25th January 2019, Dam B1 in Brumadinho, Brazil, suddenly collapsed and produced a catastrophic tailings flow with severe human, environmental and infrastructural consequences. Previous numerical back-analyses of the tailings flow have relied on deterministic approaches, which provide useful reference results but do not explicitly incorporate uncertainty associated to rupture hydrograph and tailings' physical properties. This work presents a probabilistic approach to study the tailings dam-breach flow caused by the rupture of Dam B1, focusing on the quantification and interpretation of the effects of input uncertainty on hazard-related hydrodynamical outputs. Deterministic data was obtained through HEC-RAS v6.6 by considering tailings as an one-phase Bingham fluid. The probabilistic framework combines dimensionality reduction, metamodeling and flooding classification to perform fast prediction of unexplored input scenarios. It allows to obtain data distributions that reflect output uncertainty and to estimate variance-based sensitivity indices to quantify the influence of input uncertainty over output variability. Results show that uncertainty is strongly dependent on time and spatial location. Hydrograph-related parameters mainly control the timing and magnitude of the early flow, whereas yield stress becomes more influential in regions associated with flow attenuation, spreading and possible arrest. Overall, the framework provides probabilistic hazard estimates and insights into the physical mechanisms governing the dynamics of tailings flow.

papers.title: Entropy of a Zipfian Distributed Lexicon
papers.abstract: This article presents the calculation of the entropy of a system with Zipfian distribution and shows that a communication system tends to present an exponent value close to one, but still greater than one, so that it might maximize entropy and hold a feasible lexicon with an increasing size. This result is in agreement with what is observed in natural languages and with the balance between the speaker and listener communication efforts. On the other hand, the entropy of the communicating source is very sensitive to the exponent value as well as the length of the observable data, making it a poor parameter to characterize the communication process.

papers.title: Inferring Neural Activity Changes under Recording Uncertainty with Transformers and Variational Inference
papers.abstract: A difference in recorded firing rate across days may reflect a change in neuronal activity, missed spikes or recording a different neuron. We present a statistical approach that combines neuron tracking with Bayesian estimates of stationary mean recorded firing rates. Bounds under assumed differences in spike detection connect recorded rates to biological rate changes. We assess recording loss and uncertainty in rate changes in simulations, and count-model fit in recordings. We also compare two transformer estimators with Gaussian and flow variational inference under a shared temporal negative-binomial model. Flow variational inference agrees most closely with reference posteriors, while predictive performance varies across mice. Rate-change intervals contain true simulated changes less often than intended. In UnitMatch recordings from five mice, some inferred changes remain supported when spike detection is allowed to differ between days; others depend on equal detection. These interpretations require a correct neuron match. The approach identifies which inferred rate changes remain supported under specified recording assumptions and where uncertainty limits interpretation.

papers.title: Spatial Extremes on Domains with Physical Barriers
papers.abstract: We propose a model for spatial extremes what realistically accommodates nonconvex domains. Most existing models assume that tail dependence between locations depends only on their separation. Even if extended to be anisotropic or nonstationary, they still cannot accommodate features between points that may mediate the dependence. This assumption limits their applicability in settings where physical barriers like mountains, coastlines, or islands may attenuate or even block dependence in extreme events. In this work, we use the idea of a visibility graph to modify an existing spatial random scale model. This results in a tail dependence model that naturally accommodates nonconvex spatial domains, where the nonconvex features are interpreted as physical barriers. Furthermore, the model inherits key properties from the scale mixture like the ability to represent asymptotic independence at long ranges and either asymptotic dependence or asymptotic independence at short ranges. We apply our model to two applications in which physical barriers feature prominently in determining the spatial structure of extreme events. The first is precipitation in the South Island of New Zealand, where the Southern Alps shelter the eastern region from the effects of atmospheric rivers which arrive from the west. The second is significant wave heights in the North Atlantic, where the Faroe Islands tend to block the effects of extratropical cyclones traveling into the North Sea.

papers.title: Sensor Monitoring Towards Industry 4.0: Bridging Concepts on the $C_n$ Multivariate Control Chart
papers.abstract: The main challenge in monitoring multiple sensors is the high dimensionality that a process can easily reach. From a decision-making perspective, converting these multivariate dynamics into an informative visualization is also not trivial. Statistical Process Control (SPC) techniques detect changes in quality characteristics, but they are difficult to apply beyond the normality (Gaussian) assumption. For instance, the most well-known SPC multivariate control chart is based on Hotelling's $T^2$ statistic, which assumes that the process data follow a multivariate normal distribution (which rarely occurs in practice) and that the observations are serially independent. This study focuses on the multivariate case (dimension $d \geq 2$), regardless of the data dependence or marginal asymmetry. We propose a new control chart for change detection in copula-based multivariate processes, called the $C_n$-chart, which is based on a density level-set tolerance region built from a copula function, and we derive its run-length properties. The methodology also quantifies the (not necessarily linear) dependence among the variables. Two case studies are presented, one on water quality control and the other on monitoring brass-steel thermostats, complemented by a simulation study of run-length performance and computational cost. The results show that the proposed methodology captures both the association among variables and the anomalies, and that it accommodates variable selection through conditional (regression) modeling of the margins.

papers.title: Laplace Bayesian transport maps for generative modeling of non-Gaussian climate fields
papers.abstract: Transport maps provide a powerful framework for the generative modeling of complex, non-Gaussian spatial fields, such as those encountered in climate science. By mapping a complicated target distribution to a standard Gaussian reference distribution, they can serve as efficient stochastic surrogates. However, current Bayesian transport maps, which are modeled using autoregressive Gaussian processes, typically rely on empirical Bayes estimates that ignore hyperparameter uncertainty. Here, we contrast this point-estimate approach with a fully Bayesian model that provides posterior uncertainty quantification in transport map hyperparameters. To avoid the high cost of Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), we also propose a Laplace approximation to the hyperparameter posteriors, which can be computed at negligible additional computational cost relative to empirical Bayes. We provide numerical evidence and a real-data climate application demonstrating that these Laplace approximations can accurately capture most posterior summaries at a fraction of the cost of MCMC, while maintaining good predictive properties. Thus, our approach offers a scalable, uncertainty-aware framework for the generative modeling of non-Gaussian climate fields.

papers.title: Bayesian Computation of Copula-based Multivariate Models with an Application to Doping Detection
papers.abstract: The Athlete Biological Passport (ABP) monitors athletes for doping by comparing their biomarker readings against personalized reference ranges. These are estimated via the Bayesian ADAPTIVE model, which analyzes biomarkers separately and ignores their dependence. Building on a recently proposed copula-based multivariate extension of ADAPTIVE, this paper focuses on its computational aspects, introducing a fully joint MCMC algorithm and comparing it with a two-step Bayesian IFM estimator. Simulations show the two procedures perform comparably under a correctly specified copula, but exhibit a genuine trade-off under misspecification: the Bayesian IFM protects marginal inference, while the joint MCMC yields better-calibrated dependence estimates and is markedly faster. The two approaches are tested on a dataset containing ABP profiles of elite athletes, provided by NADO Italia, and collected as part of the project {\it Enhancing the methodological framework for doping detection: from univariate to multivariate testing analysis on Athlete Biological Passport profiles}. Both approaches achieve consistent classification performance, providing anti-doping organizations with two concrete inferential routes for adopting a multivariate ADAPTIVE model, along with guidance on the trade-offs between them.

papers.title: Assessing model calibration with boosting trees
papers.abstract: The main goal in regression modelling consists in approximating the conditional mean of a response given a set of features. A regression function is said to be strongly calibrated if the resulting mean estimates match the true conditional means for almost every set of features. Aiming for strong calibration seems not achievable in practice as one typically deals with finite samples of noisy observations. A weaker notion of calibration is auto-calibration, and it means that the conditional expectation of the response, given a mean estimate, matches this estimate. This notion is important, e.g., in insurance pricing as it ensures no cross-subsidization between different price cohorts. In this paper, we show that boosting trees can be used to test necessary conditions for strong calibration and auto-calibration, respectively. The practical relevance of our approach is supported by a numerical example, in which the proposed tests achieve high empirical power.

papers.title: A Physically Informed Changepoint Score for Fault Prioritisation in District Heating
papers.abstract: Poorly cooling district-heating installations raise return temperatures and pumped flow, increasing heat losses and pumping energy and hindering low-temperature operation. Faults often go unreported for weeks, so their onset is unknown and energy is wasted in the meantime. Utilities flag poorly cooling installations by a low supply-return temperature difference, but not when the problem began. Changepoint detectors such as the Bayesian Estimator of Abrupt Change, Seasonality, and Trend (BEAST) can date a change but report only its probability, so a large, fault-like change and a marginal one can look alike. We therefore develop a decision score that weighs each BEAST change in temperature difference and flow by its probability, size, deviation from recent operation and physical direction. Joint falls in temperature difference and rises in flow, the signature of insufficient cooling, rank first. Across 1,522 cases, 648 with a reported fault, 24 of the 25 highest-ranked cases were reported faults, and Average Precision was 0.772 against a prevalence of 0.426, likely conservative, as unreported cases may contain faults. Without using the report date, the strongest flow rise in reported-fault cases came a median of 11 days before the report (128 days in comparison cases). Combined with temperature-difference screening, the score raised Average Precision in season-matched cases from 0.486 to 0.646. After the detected change, flagged reported-fault installations returned water 16 K warmer and about half their circulated water delivered no heat. The score gives utilities a short list for inspection and a candidate onset date for each change.
